## Two minutes of music, thirty-two notes

A two-minute piece doesn't need two minutes of unrelated note data. Repetition
gives your listener something to hold, and having something to hold is what
makes a departure legible in the first place. When the opening comes back after
contrasting material, it arrives carrying both its original identity and all the
time that passed while it was away.

*Form* is how sections are organised across the span of a piece. Binary form
works in two large regions. Ternary form returns, as in ABA. Rondo alternates a
recurring A against contrasting episodes. For building one, treat a section like
a function and the form plan like its call sequence. A varied return then means
invoking familiar material with different arguments, and never means copying the
section and editing the copy.

## A plan, and the sections it calls

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 60
use_synth :prophet

sections = {
  a: [:c4, :e4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :f4, :g4, :c5],
  b: [:a3, :c4, :e4, :g4, :f4, :d4, :b3, :g3],
  c: [:f4, :a4, :g4, :e4, :d4, :b3, :c4, :e4],
  transition: [:g3, :a3, :b3, :d4, :f4, :e4, :d4, :g3]
}

define :play_section do |notes, transpose, amp|
  notes.each do |pitch|
    play note(pitch) + transpose, sustain: 2.5,
      release: 0.35, amp: amp
    sleep 3
  end
end

form = [
  [:a, 0, 0.65],
  [:b, 0, 0.55],
  [:a, 12, 0.5],
  [:transition, 0, 0.6],
  [:c, 0, 0.7]
]

form.each do |name, transpose, amp|
  puts "section #{name} transpose=#{transpose}"
  play_section sections[name], transpose, amp
end
```

Each section runs twenty-four beats, so five calls fill two minutes at 60 BPM.
Set a timer if you like; this one takes a while. When A returns it comes back an
octave higher and quieter. The note data says it's the same section, and the
arguments let the elapsed time leave a mark on it.

The transition gets its own name because connecting two regions is a real formal
job. It isn't an anonymous gap between the parts that matter.

## Rearrange the plan, not the notes

1. Call A twice before B. The opening gets more time to settle into memory and
   contrast gets postponed. Does the second pass strengthen your recognition of
   A, or start to wear the eight notes out?
2. Bring A back at its original register and amplitude. Compare that literal
   return against the quieter octave version. In one of them recognition wins
   and in the other change does, and which is which will surprise you less than
   how large the difference is.
3. Change the plan to A-B-A-C-A. More frequent returns pull the design toward
   rondo, and C becomes an episode framed by familiar material on both sides.

Each of those is one line in `form`. None of them touches a note.

## Why the plan is data

The `sections` hash stores each body of material exactly once. The `form` array
records order and realisation arguments, and `play_section` interprets both.
Large-scale revision happens in a short, visible plan, with no duplicated note
lists anywhere. Change A at the source and every one of its returns stays
related to it, automatically.

A section name is a claim about identity; its arguments describe the variation.
Transposition preserves interval relationships while moving register, and
amplitude changes where the listener seems to be standing. Other arguments could
select instrumentation, articulation, or which phrases to leave out. Push far
enough and you reach a real question: if variation erases every recognisable
feature of a section, giving it a new name describes what you actually hear
better than insisting it's still A.

The control-flow analogy has a limit, and it's worth being precise about where.
A listener hears a return through memory of everything that happened in between.
A runtime attaches no weight whatsoever to the second call of a function. The
analogy is a construction tool, not a theory of listening: define reusable
units, order them, parameterise the changes you consider legitimate, and keep
that plan separate from rendering.

Code boundaries also need audible evidence, which is the trap here. A new key,
register, texture, cadence or rhythmic profile announces B. Changing a symbol in
an array announces nothing at all. If B behaves like A, your listener hears one
long section and your form plan is a private fiction. The printed labels are for
inspection; someone who can't see the log should still hear the divisions.

Proportion carries meaning too. That transition lasts as long as A, B and C do,
which is long enough that it stops sounding like a bridge and starts sounding
like a fourth section. Shorten it to four notes and listen again to what it
seems to be doing. Formal labels are analytical judgements resting on proportion
and behaviour. Your renderer doesn't enforce them, and it won't warn you.

Distance in time changes repetition as well. A return after twenty seconds feels
like immediate confirmation. After a minute, the same notes feel recovered from
somewhere. Keeping the order in a visible array makes those spans measurable and
cheap to revise. The call doesn't change. Its position hands it a different
formal consequence.

## Build a rondo you can hear the seams in

Compose an A-B-A-C-A rondo of at least ninety seconds. Store A once and render
its returns with two different argument sets. Give B and C distinct pitch ranges
and rhythmic profiles, so the contrast survives with the labels switched off.
Keep the form as data, include one named transition, and copy no section arrays.

Then run it twice. The first time, print each section name as it plays. The
second time, comment the `puts` out, listen straight through, and mark where you
hear the boundaries. Compare your marks against the plan. Every boundary you
missed is a place where your form exists in the array and not in the air, and
that gap is the only thing this exercise is really measuring.
